passage: Chaitanya had the whole plan sketched on the back of a bus ticket: cycle the twenty kilometres to the waterfall on Sunday, swim, back by dark. "You're coming, right?" he asked Joseph outside the village shop. Joseph turned the ticket over, one eyebrow up. "Maybe." "Maybe? You're scared." Joseph shrugged, and Chaitanya nearly pushed harder, then noticed Joseph didn't look scared so much as thoughtful; he was frowning at the sky over the hills, where clouds were already stacking up. "Okay," Chaitanya said. "What's the maybe about?" "The radio said heavy rain from Saturday. Last monsoon the stream near the fall rose in an hour. And my back brake is half gone." He paused. "And yes, a bit scared. Both." Chaitanya chewed on that. "So... next Sunday, if it's dry, and we fix your brake first at Salim's shop?" Joseph's eyebrow came down. "Now that's a yes."

qa.q: How far is the waterfall?
qa.a: The waterfall is twenty kilometres away.

qa.q: What feelings were behind Joseph's 'Maybe'?
qa.a: Joseph's doubt was mostly careful thinking about heavy rain, the rising stream and a weak brake, mixed with some honest fear, as the word 'Both' admits.

qa.q: What turned the 'maybe' into a yes?
qa.a: Chaitanya stopped pushing, asked what the maybe was about, and changed the plan to a dry Sunday with the brake fixed first. 👍

qa.q: How did Chaitanya first read the raised eyebrow?
qa.a: Chaitanya first took it as fear and nearly pushed harder, before noticing Joseph was watching the clouds.

grounding: It shows a teenager's hesitation and 'maybe' reflecting both careful thinking and fear, and open discussion working better than pressure.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: Pema, you say your study group looks bored when you explain? Let me tell you about your Jeevan Tata at fifteen. I was in charge of our group's model of the heart, and I was very proud of my explanations. There was a boy called Nanda who sat through them rubbing his eyes, chin on his fist. I decided he was bored, maybe even mocking me, so I started talking faster and louder at him. Sister Agnes, our science teacher, watched this for a day. Then she said, "Jeevan, you have not asked him one thing." So I asked him, a bit rudely, "Are you even following?" Nanda went red and said, "No. I got lost at the valves on Monday and was too ashamed to say." The fist under the chin was him trying to keep up. After that I stopped every few minutes and asked, "Where are you?" Your face tells me you are interested now. But I will ask anyway: are you?

qa.q: What was Jeevan in charge of in the group?
qa.a: Jeevan was in charge of the group's model of the heart.

qa.q: What was young Jeevan feeling when he decided Nanda was bored?
qa.a: Jeevan felt proud of the explanations and then irritated, even slighted, thinking he was being mocked, which made him talk faster and louder.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Asking Nanda directly, after Sister Agnes pointed it out, revealed confusion, and stopping every few minutes to ask 'Where are you?' kept the group with him.

qa.q: What was it like for Nanda during those explanations?
qa.a: Nanda had been lost since Monday and was ashamed to say so, rubbing his eyes and propping his chin while trying to keep up.

grounding: It shows a teenager misreading a classmate's face as boredom when it was confusion, told as an elder's memory in which asking beats assuming.

passage:
Wednesday!!!
I'm still not sure it's real. At 4:30 the list for the state science camp went up on the notice board, and I only went to look because Maria dragged me. I was ready to be sad for her. Then she grabbed my wrist and pointed. My name. Disha Kulkarni, fourth line. I just stood there. My mouth was open and no sound came out, and my hands went cold, like stepping into the sea. I read it five times. I didn't cry or jump or anything, I just kept staring and my brain went completely white. Maria didn't shout "party!" or make me talk. She walked me to the bench under the gulmohar and sat there with me for maybe ten minutes while I held my water bottle and breathed. Then, out of nowhere, I laughed so hard I got hiccups. Told Aai at dinner. She dropped a spoon.

qa.q: What time did the list go up?
qa.a: The list went up on the notice board at 4:30.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling while staring at the list?
qa.a: Disha was astonished, frozen with mouth open and cold hands, too stunned to feel the joy yet; it came later as the hiccupping laugh.

qa.q: What did Maria do that helped?
qa.a: Maria didn't push for celebration or talk but walked Disha to the bench and sat quietly for ten minutes, giving the shock room to settle. 🙂

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when she saw Disha's name?
qa.a: Maria was clearly thrilled for Disha, grabbing Disha's wrist and pointing, yet chose calm company over noise once Disha froze.

grounding: It shows a teenager freezing and staring at unexpected good news, astonishment stronger than surprise, and quiet space letting the joy arrive.

subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
passage: Outside the community centre's office, Pankaj sat on a plastic chair with his file on his knees, bouncing one leg. It was his first real interview, for a summer helper job at the children's library. His heart was hammering so hard he could feel it in his ears. Rehana, a college volunteer who ran the reading hour, sat down beside him with a cup of chai. "Nervous?" "Very. Also I really want it. Is that weird? Both at once?" "Not weird at all. Here's a trick I use before exams. Scared and excited feel almost the same in the body, same fast heart. So say it out loud: I'm excited." Pankaj laughed. "That's silly." "Try it." "I'm... excited." He said it again, a bit louder. His leg slowed. The heart kept racing, but it felt less like a warning and more like a drumroll. When the door opened and the librarian called his name, he stood up and said, "Ready."

qa.q: What job was Pankaj interviewing for?
qa.a: A summer helper job at the children's library.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling as he bounced his leg?
qa.a: Pankaj felt nervous and eager at once, heart hammering; the same racing heart carried both worry about the interview and wanting the job badly.

qa.q: How did Rehana's trick help?
qa.a: Naming the racing heart as excitement turned the nervous energy into readiness, so his leg slowed and it felt like a drumroll instead of a warning.

qa.q: Why might Rehana understand the mix so well?
qa.a: Rehana had used the same trick before exams, so she recognised the blend of nerves and eagerness and treated it as normal, not weird.

grounding: It shows a teenager feeling eager and anxious at once before a first interview, and labelling the racing heart as excitement turning it into readiness.

passage:
Saturday night
WE WON. Inter-school quiz final, 180 to 175, on the very last question. When Yash buzzed and said "Tungabhadra" and the quizmaster said "Correct!", I screamed, actually screamed, pumped both fists, and we hugged in a big sweaty heap on the stage. My cheeks hurt from grinning. Then I did a not-great thing. The St Mark's team had been smug all day, and their captain had said "good luck, you'll need it" in the morning. So I looked right at her and mouthed "need it?" with my eyebrows up. Everyone on our side laughed. And then I saw she was blinking really fast, trying not to cry in front of the whole hall. My stomach dropped. I walked over, shook her hand and said, "Closest final ever. Your team was brilliant on the science round." She said thanks, still wobbly. Yash said, "Vidya, that was the right thing." Still grinning though. 180!

qa.q: What was the final score?
qa.a: The final score was 180 to 175.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling after mouthing 'need it?'
qa.a: Vidya was triumphant and a bit smug at first, then felt a sinking guilt on seeing the captain blinking back tears.

qa.q: How did Vidya turn the moment around?
qa.a: Vidya walked over, shook the captain's hand and praised the science round, sharing the win graciously instead of gloating.

qa.q: What was the win like for the St Mark's captain?
qa.a: For the captain it was a painful loss made worse by being mocked in front of the hall, so she was close to tears.

grounding: It shows a teenager's fist-pumping triumph after a win, a moment of gloating that hurts a rival, and the win then being shared graciously.

passage: I sit behind Saurabh in maths, so I've had two years of his face, which never moves. On Monday Kashish came in with a new short haircut, and Saurabh looked at her for a long second and said, completely flat, "Bold. Very brave choice." No smile. No eyebrow. Nothing. Half the row laughed, because with Saurabh that's usually a joke. Kashish didn't. She touched the back of her neck and sat down slowly. From where I sat, I honestly couldn't tell if he meant it as a compliment, a joke or a dig. I don't think Kashish could either. At break she turned round and asked him straight: "Was that a joke or a dig? I really can't tell with you." Saurabh blinked. For the first time in two years I saw his face do something; it looked worried. "Joke. Compliment joke. It looks good. Sorry, I forget people can't read me." Kashish nodded. "Maybe smile next time."

qa.q: What did Saurabh say about the haircut?
qa.a: He said, completely flat, "Bold. Very brave choice."

qa.q: What might Kashish have been feeling when she touched the back of her neck?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt self-conscious and a little hurt, unsure whether the flat comment was a dig at the new haircut; it could also have been simple confusion.

qa.q: Why was Kashish's direct question a good move?
qa.a: Deadpan gives no cues, so asking 'Was that a joke or a dig?' settled it quickly and let Saurabh explain it was a compliment.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see his own comment?
qa.a: Saurabh meant it as a joking compliment and was worried to realise people can't read his flat face.

grounding: It shows a deadpan remark that listeners cannot read as joke or insult, seen by an observer, and a direct question settling it.

passage: In their Toronto apartment, dinner had become a one-word show. "How was school, Xin?" "Fine." "Swimming?" "Fine." Then the phone came out, and Xin's eyes stayed on it until the plates were cleared. Ivan, who had married Xin's mother two years before, felt the old urge to say "You're being rude," and swallowed it. He didn't know if Xin was tired, sad, private or just bored with him. So he tried something slower. Every evening he knocked once, said, "Making hot chocolate, want one?" and left it at that. Most nights the answer was "No." On the ninth night it was "Okay." On the twelfth, Xin sat on the kitchen stool while the milk heated and said, without looking up, "Morning practice is at five now. And everyone in Vancouver has stopped replying." Ivan nodded, stirred, and didn't lecture. "That's a lot at once," he said. Xin took the mug. "Yeah."

qa.q: What time is morning practice now?
qa.a: Morning practice is at five now.

qa.q: What might Xin have been feeling behind the one-word answers?
qa.a: Xin was likely exhausted from the early practice and lonely, hurt that old friends in Vancouver had stopped replying; from outside it could have looked like boredom or rudeness.

qa.q: Why did the hot chocolate routine work better than calling Xin rude?
qa.a: It offered a low-pressure chance to connect every evening without accusation, so after twelve nights Xin was ready to say what was going on.

qa.q: What was dinner like for Ivan during those weeks?
qa.a: Ivan felt shut out and tempted to scold, unsure whether the silence was about him, but chose patience instead.

grounding: It shows a teenager's withdrawal and single-word answers having unclear causes, and patient check-ins over time working better than accusations.

passage: The school bus was packed and deafening, forty kids and a broken window rattling, when the drama teacher's message landed in the class group: the cast list for the annual play. Everyone crowded round phones. "Charu, you're not Portia! Nikita got it!" someone yelled over the noise. Heads turned to see her face. Charu kept it perfectly still. She shrugged one shoulder, said, "Cool," and went back to looking out at the traffic. Only Irawati, squashed beside her, noticed her thumbnail pressing a crescent into her palm. Irawati said nothing on the bus; there was no quiet corner in that noise and too many ears. At the stop, as the others ran off, she fell into step with Charu. "I've got nowhere to be for an hour," she said. "Samosa? You can talk or not talk." They walked two blocks before Charu said, very quietly, "I practised that speech for a month." Then her face finally moved.

qa.q: Who got the part of Portia?
qa.a: Nikita got it.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling behind the still face?
qa.a: Charu was most likely hurt and disappointed, as the thumbnail pressing into the palm hints, but hid it on the crowded bus; there may also have been pride in not showing it.

qa.q: How did Irawati offer a chance to talk?
qa.a: Irawati waited for quiet and privacy, then offered time and a samosa with no pressure: 'You can talk or not talk.'

qa.q: How might the others on the bus have read Charu's shrug?
qa.a: They probably thought Charu didn't care much, since the face stayed still and the answer was just 'Cool'.

grounding: It shows a teenager keeping a blank face to hide disappointment from peers, and a trusted person offering a private chance to talk.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Trisha knew the exact moment it would happen. Mrs Sen would say, "Trisha, your answer?" and heat would climb her neck like a tide, and she would be sure the whole Kolkata classroom could see it. Last week she had whispered "I don't know" just to make it stop, though she did know. At home that evening Sharmila, back from college for the weekend, watched her rehearse the next day's answer in the mirror, already pink. "Okay, three things," Sharmila said. "Breathe out slowly before you speak, longer out than in. Then look at something outside yourself, the blackboard or Mrs Sen's chalk, not at your own face in your head. And honestly? Most people are busy thinking about their own answers. They barely notice." Trisha rolled her eyes but tried it. Next morning, when her name came, she breathed out, fixed her eyes on the chalk and gave the answer. Her cheeks still warmed. But the boy beside her was busy drawing a cricket bat, and nobody said a word.

qa.q: What did Trisha whisper last week?
qa.a: Trisha whispered "I don't know", though she did know.

qa.q: What was Trisha afraid of when her name was called?
qa.a: Trisha was anxious about being seen blushing, sure the whole class could see the heat on her neck; it may also have been fear of getting the answer wrong.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's steps helped, and how?
qa.a: Breathing out slowly, fixing her eyes on the chalk and remembering others are busy with their own answers eased the distress enough for Trisha to answer.

qa.q: How did the classmates react when Trisha answered?
qa.a: They barely noticed; the boy beside her was busy drawing a cricket bat, and nobody said a word.

grounding: It shows a teenager who blushes easily fearing being noticed, and slow breathing, outward focus and remembering others rarely notice reducing the distress.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Uday, sit. You asked what to do when your friend cried in class. Your Yogesh Chacha has a story about that. When I was sixteen, on results day, my friend Harpal came out of the school office and started crying at the bus stop, big tears, wiping them with his sleeve. I decided he had failed. So I started talking fast: "It's okay, the re-exam is easy, my cousin also failed, don't worry." He looked at me like I was mad. Finally he said, "I passed. Maths also. I was sure I would fail it." Those were relief tears, and I had given him a whole speech about failing! After that I learned. The next time I saw someone crying, a girl in my tuition class, I just sat next to her and asked, "Do you want company, or quiet?" She said she was so angry with her brother she could cry. Angry tears. See? Same water, different reasons. So ask, and stay.

qa.q: Where did Harpal start crying?
qa.a: Harpal started crying at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was young Yogesh feeling when he started talking fast?
qa.a: Yogesh felt worried and eager to comfort, sure Harpal had failed, which made him rush into reassurance instead of asking.

qa.q: Which choice in the story worked better, and why?
qa.a: With the girl at tuition, young Yogesh sat down and asked 'Do you want company, or quiet?', which let her explain the tears were anger instead of him guessing.

qa.q: What was it like for Harpal to hear the speech about failing?
qa.a: Harpal was confused, looking at Yogesh as if he were mad, because the tears were relief, not sadness.

grounding: It shows a teenager misreading a friend's tears as sadness when they were relief, and learning through an elder's story to ask gently and stay present.
